paras: The lynching of Santos Salizer was the reported hanging of a Mexican man near Collins, in Nueces County, Texas, on the night of Sunday, January 22, 1888. He was accused of murdering Jacob Stafford, a sheep raiser whose body had been found in a water hole the day before. The story reached Corpus Christi only as a report, yet it ran in papers across the country, several of which headlined the slight evidence on which he was said to have been killed.

According to a Corpus Christi special to the Atlanta Constitution, Jake Stafford was "a German" and "a peaceable man" in the sheep business who lived a few miles outside Collins. He left Collins for home at three o'clock on a Thursday afternoon and never arrived, and after his wife raised the alarm a search began the next morning. His body was found on Saturday in a water hole with three bullet wounds, one through the body and two through the head. The wire version instead placed the water hole "back of his house" and said the body was "riddled with bullets." Because the nine dollars Stafford had carried were missing, the Constitution's correspondent concluded that robbery was the motive.

Suspicion fell on Santos Salizer, whom the Constitution described as "a Mexican of bad character." In the wire account, sent from Corpus Christi on January 24 as a special to the Galveston News, the case against him rested on the tracks of a horse he had ridden, which "corresponded with tracks found near the body." On that evidence, the dispatch said, he "was hunted down and hanged by ranchmen and cowboys" on Sunday night.

The Constitution's special, dated a day earlier, gave a different sequence. In its version Salizer had been arrested on suspicion, and on the morning of January 23 a rumor reached Corpus Christi that a mob had hanged him the night before. Neither account named any member of the lynching party.
Every account presented the hanging as a report or rumor that had reached Corpus Christi, and no later dispatch confirming or denying it, or reporting an inquest or arrests, appears in the coverage.

The Galveston News special was reprinted widely on January 25, appearing in the New York Sun, the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Waterbury Evening Democrat and the Beatrice Daily Express, among others. Headlines ranged from the neutral "Lynched a Mexican" and "Suspected of Murder" to the Wichita Eagle's "Mexican Murderer Hanged" and the Washington Evening Star's "Betrayed by His Horse's Hoofs," both of which treated the accusation as settled. Other editors pointed to the thin case: the Emporia Weekly News headed the item "Mighty Thin Evidence," and the Waterbury paper chose "Judge Lynch Accepts Slim Evidence." The Mitchell Capital in Dakota called it a "Lynching Bee in Texas."

Two German-language dailies, the Illinois Staats-Zeitung and Der Deutsche Correspondent, ran translated versions the same day, the Staats-Zeitung saying he had been hanged by farmers and herdsmen and betrayed by his horse's hoofprints. A condensed digest item, printed by the Kenosha Telegraph and later by the Mower County Transcript and The Progress, dated the lynching "the 24th" and placed Collins in "Mex." A week after the event, the Atlanta Constitution printed its own Corpus Christi special under "Crimes and Criminals," headed "A German Shepherd is Murdered for His Money," in the same column as a report of a triple lynching in North Carolina. Every version identified Salizer as "a Mexican," and several put the word in the headline.

The accounts differ on whether Salizer was in custody: the Constitution's special said he had been arrested on suspicion before the mob hanged him, while the wire said ranchmen and cowboys hunted him down. The digest item's date and its "Collins, Mex." conflict with the Texas datelines, which place the hanging near Collins in Nueces County on Sunday night; the digest appears to have used the date of the dispatch. His name was spelled differently from paper to paper, as "Santas Salizer," "Santos Saliser," "Santosear Salizar" and "SANTOS SOLIZER."

reader.title: Lynching of Santos Salizer
bases: A Mexican man accused of murder was reported hunted down and hanged by 'ranchmen and cowboys' (A2, A3), or hanged by a mob after his arrest (A12).

Every account says Salizer was hanged without legal process by 'ranchmen and cowboys' or 'a mob' for the supposed murder of Jacob Stafford (A1, A3, A12), which meets the definition; but the hanging is known only as a report or rumor reaching Corpus Christi, and no confirming dispatch was found (A1, A12).

Two separate Corpus Christi dispatches, the Galveston News special (A1, A3) and the Atlanta Constitution special (A12), agree that Salizer was hanged for Stafford's murder, though both relay an unconfirmed report and differ on whether he had been arrested.

accounts.gist: A report reached Corpus Christi that Salizer was lynched Sunday night near Collins; tracks of a horse he rode matched tracks near Stafford's body, and on this evidence he was hunted down and hanged by ranchmen and cowboys.

accounts.label: Atlanta Constitution special from Corpus Christi
accounts.gist: Stafford, a peaceable German sheep man, was murdered and robbed on his way home from Collins; Salizar, 'a Mexican of bad character,' was arrested on suspicion, and a rumor said he was hung by a mob the night before.

accounts.label: Digest item
accounts.gist: Santos Solizer, a Mexican, was lynched on the 24th at 'Collins, Mex.' for the supposed murder of Jacob Stafford.

framing.detail: The Wichita Eagle headed the wire 'Mexican Murderer Hanged,' treating the accusation as fact.
The Emporia Weekly News ('Mighty Thin Evidence') and Waterbury Evening Democrat ('Judge Lynch Accepts Slim Evidence') headlined the weakness of the horse-track evidence.

The Sun, St. Paul Daily Globe, Beatrice Daily Express and others ran the wire under neutral heads such as 'Lynched a Mexican' and 'Suspected of Murder'; the Mitchell Capital used 'Lynching Bee in Texas.'
The Atlanta Constitution centered Stafford's murder under 'A German Shepherd is Murdered for His Money' and called the suspect 'a Mexican of bad character.'
The Evening Star's 'Betrayed by his Horse's Hoofs' presented the track evidence as decisive.

versions.value: Hunted down and hanged by ranchmen and cowboys (not in custody)
Arrested on suspicion, then hung by a mob

conflicts.note: Both are second-hand Corpus Christi reports; the Constitution special (Jan. 23) is earlier, the wire (Jan. 24) more detailed. Neither names who arrested him or held him.
The digest item took the dispatch date; the Texas datelines agree on Sunday night.
'Mex.' in the digest item is a garble of the Texas story, not a Mexican location.
